It’s the same for programming competitions and solving clear-cut math problems; the model’s generalization ability goes far beyond its direct training. OpenAI's model wasn't built by grinding through other. millennium prize problems; it was trained on vast amounts of easier math and then directly transferred to unsolved ones. It’s hard to predict this in advance, but he estimates there is at least a 25%chance that this won't be achieved until after 2030. But conversely, it could be much faster. models also points to around 2027. Then the most direct inference is that we will reach extreme superintelligence within a year. He says this question is even more important than how fast the initial speed is. speed at which ideas get harder to find , we will see what is called a "pure software takeoff." The processes for these tasks require interaction with the real world and cannot be replicated in a server room. His answer is not to expect to. bake the answers to every real-world problem directly into the model, but rather to focus on the ability to quickly master new situations, even in these hard-to-verify fields. Accomplishing tasks requires two things : domain knowledge and a set of more general skills—the kind that capable people share, such as finding relevant information, planning, pushing forward through errors and obstacles, documenting what is learned, and collaborating with others. open-ended. AI will have to learn to navigate an unimaginably large number of virtual worlds; compared to today’s video games, these would be like a Bugatti compared to a horse-drawn carriage. For instance, throw an AI into a simulated economy with millions of other AIs and task it with co-founding a successful company. It won't just dwell on idealized company structures; instead , it will undergo the equivalent of centuries of corporate competition to. figure out the best ways to organize. Our general cognitive architecture was shaped by evolution, and evolution is a very crude optimization process that simply passes on a set of standard genes. In the ancestral environment, the task of this. standard was hunting, avoiding predators , and maintaining tribal status; these are only a tiny fraction of the tasks humans can handle today. Napoleon was 27 when he had already defeated much larger armies of European powers, and Rockefeller had only been in the oil industry for two years before running one of the world's largest refineries. They did need experience, but it took years, not decades. Whatever happened in their minds, AI should be able to replicate or even surpass it; there is no reason to. believe humans have reached the ceiling for how fast one can learn from experience. Moreover, AI has another advantage: it can accumulate years of deployment experience in just a few calendar days. If you want a future AI to manage a Fortune 500 company better than the current CEO, how long would it take to get up to speed? On the first morning, have it shadow the CEO, and it could read every email, every instant message, and every document in the company's history. By the end of the first day, its multiple avatars could have interviewed every employee and major client. It indeed cannot access feedback that requires months of waiting.

, such as next quarter's financial results, but even with this limitation, he still expects such AI to reach top-tier human levels in all fields within months of its development. According to his median scenario, that is something that will happen in 2028 or 2029. And the story doesn't end there; even if progress at the software level gradually plateaus, AI will continue to improve by increasing computing power. Over the past five years, even without any AI assistance, global AI computing power has roughly tripled every year. AI created by sparks will be particularly adept at helping us continue to scale up. compute—for example, by designing new AI chips, planning new power plants, or even remotely controlling robots to build facilities and data centers. The only difference is that this path takes years to reach the same destination that purely hardware-based approaches could reach in just a few months. This superintelligence, which relates to humans as we relate to chimpanzees—for this video, I’ve included a technical argument at the end to explain why AI research is, in principle, verifiable. This part is a bit hard-core, so I’ll summarize the key points for you. AI R& D is roughly divided into three main areas: pre-training, post-training, and inference efficiency, each with concrete metrics that can serve directly as. training objectives. These three areas combined perfectly cover the entirety of algorithmic progress. So, it’s not surprising that overall AI progress can be used as a training objective; since AI training happens inside data centers , the things we do to improve models are exactly what data centers can measure. First, let’s look at pre-training: you can set a target for a model to reach a fixed loss on a small-scale model using as little compute as possible. Loss on a test set is a measurable value, very easy to verify, and even rankable. You can design an environment to see if the model can predict whether algorithmic. improvements that work at one parameter scale will still hold true at a scale of 10 billion parameters. Post-training also has proxy metrics, such as dropping a model into an environment it has never seen to see how quickly it adapts to achieve good results; ByteDance’s AdaBench benchmark measures exactly this type of capability. Inside ByteDance, there is also a benchmark called "C," which contains about 500 real-world problems that their researchers and engineers have solved this year. Every benchmark is also a reinforcement learning environment, which essentially tasks the model with replicating the frontier progress humans have made in the last three to six months; inference. efficiency is even easier to measure, as GPU usage, KV cache size per token, and latency are all readily available numbers. Tucked inside this is a counterintuitive piece of information: the lab Magic recently announced that they used about half the compute of the original GPT-3 to train a foundational model capable of rivaling leading open-weights models like DeepSeek-V 4 Pro. At today’s prices, that amount of compute is worth approximately $ 500,000 . So he concludes that pre-training hasn't hit a ceiling; increasing it by several orders of magnitude is entirely possible. recursive self-improvement. First point : continual learning. For the past year and a half, he has maintained that the core capability AI lacks today is learning from work experience. Every new session is like its first day on the job ; a session can only retain a few hours of information, failing to accumulate the feedback and know-how that takes weeks or months to build. In December 2025, he was still saying it was incredible that these systems, lacking even the basic learning abilities of a child, were trying to crack the AGI algorithms that have baffled humanity for over half a century. First , solving continual learning might not. require a major architectural breakthrough; scaling up in-context learning to make sessions effectively last longer, allowing a single instance to learn while it works, might be enough . Second, continual learning is itself a research problem with clear validation metrics, similar to solving a math problem. If you had asked him two years ago to compare the Navier-Stokes equations with continual learning, asking which is harder to solve, he wouldn't have thought the answer was obviously the former. His analogy is clever: current models lack long-term memory, like the clumsiest interns, yet they are already solving millennial-old problems. It's like someone moving down the track while doing cartwheels, yet. still keeping pace with Usain Bolt. Who says that doing cartwheels means they can't win the race? He conducted research with Princeton. student Jerry Han, finding that over the past six years of pre-training progress , gains from data improvements outweighed gains from model improvements by more than three times. And so-called data improvement is essentially figuring out which methods can filter existing data and generate new synthetic data to lower the loss function, which is very similar to regular AI research work. A paper published on post-training new models confirms this; they found that systematic improvements in the scale, diversity, and verifiability of synthetic data environments basically account for all observed gains. And the way these environments are constructed. is itself becoming increasingly automated. Third, experimental compute. While mathematics can produce new discoveries with just a pen and paper, AI research requires running actual experiments, burning both compute and time. As the number of researchers grows , won't the experimental compute allocated to each person become diluted ? He did the math: if labs increase their compute by more than four times each year, following this trend, by the end of 2027, OpenAI could provide 10,000 agents—the same number of agents involved in solving that millennial prize problem. Every agent would be able to be allocated enough compute to run a GPT-3 scale training session every single day. The final model in the.

original 2017 Transformer paper only used 8 P100s for three days; that amount of compute costs about 50 dollars today , which is only one ten-thousandth of the compute used to train GPT-3. If researchers like Ilya and X2 had the experimental compute to train a GPT-3 scale model every day, they might be a bit slower than they are now. But if they just sat there and couldn't produce any meaningful progress, only complaining that the cluster was too small, he would be very surprised. Moreover, the reason labs use compute the way they do today is because researchers 'time is far scarcer than compute; the annual compensation for top researchers can reach hundreds of. millions of dollars. The way we use it today doesn't show how efficient it could be once compute becomes the main bottleneck. Agent swarms have two advantages humans can't match: first, trading labor for compute—reading every training trajectory, and as soon as a task breaks, immediately stopping to rebuild the entire environment. Small-scale experiments can be run relentlessly. Before pooling compute for a large experiment, we should spend subjective decades designing the most information-dense joint experiments, then spend another subjective few decades analyzing the results to invent better scientific methods, extracting every bit of information from small experiments. The GPT-4 paper stated that they could predict the loss of the final. model using a model with 10,000 times less compute. Scaling phenomena like this allow researchers to predict optimal hyperparameters for large training runs from models 100 times smaller. He remembers a conversation with a researcher who once said: the gods above must surely follow the same principles as the ants below. After hearing the whole argument, you’ll find his position is actually more restrained than the title suggests. The median year is set to 2028, with room left for 2027 and after 2032, splitting the probability of software-only and "spark " at 50%each. What he really wants to say is that recursive self-improvement. might have already started. So, do you think his judgment is correct? Feel free to leave a comment below. Thanks for watching, and we’ll see you in the next one.

作者分析，一旦 AI 研究能力比肩頂尖人類，進展將因速度更快、智商更高、規模更大三大維度而全面提速。AI 無需休息且運算迅捷，單兵產出約為人類的 50 倍；同時，它能將每一位「研究員」的水準拉升至頂尖專家層級，並以成千上萬個代理並行推進模組化任務。最後，作者點出未來技術走向的核心拉鋸：遞歸自我提升（RSI）與「好想法愈來愈難找」之間的競速。一旦 AI 自我迭代變聰明的速度徹底壓過難題遞增的阻力，世界便可能迎來短短數月內逼近晶片物理極限的純軟體起飛，徹底重塑人類文明的科技邊界。

================================================

Hello everyone, this is Best Partners, I’m Da Fei. If you had asked Dwarkesh Patel at the start of this year how far we are from superintelligence? This podcaster, known for his in-depth conversations, would likely have said at least another decade or more. But just this past month, his judgment has taken a radical turn. He now believes AI might reach top-tier human levels in research in just a few years or even months. Moreover, once research is automated, massive breakthroughs could be compressed into a short year or so. By 2030, or even as early as next year, we could have AI. that is at least as good as top human experts in every field. I know this claim is quite radical; even he wouldn't have believed it a few months ago. In the video he released in mid-October, he explained his entire reasoning process in detail, which was incredibly informative, and today I’ll break it down for you. Let's look at three numbers already in play. An independent evaluator spent three months embedded at METAMIND, concluding that this lab’s AI progress on well-defined tasks is already twice as fast as it was a year ago. And a large part of this acceleration likely comes from their. extensive use of AI for R&D. OpenAI disclosed internal data in September this year showing that the top 10%of researchers using AI increased their daily spending on internal agents from about $ 1,000 at the start of the year to over $ 7,000 by the end of August. DeepMind also stated in September that AI now leads 26%of their research work, a figure that was under 1%back in February. With internal R&D speeds doubled, this is the first basis for his change in judgment. The second basis is mathematics; in his words, today’s AI. solves well-defined math problems like a hot knife through butter. The progress bar looks like this: 2023 models couldn't even get four-digit addition right, 2024 saw near-total failure in high school math competitions, 2025 brought International Math Olympiad gold , and earlier this year, they began tackling niche unsolved problems. And just one month before he released his video, AI solved a Millennium Prize problem in 88 hours. He quoted a line from the novel*East of Eden*: "One thing is certain about the fall of gods: they do not just fall a little; they crash to. the ground and shatter into pieces." Of course, some people are pouring cold water on this. T. B. O'Dea recently wrote: "While AI systems are starting to automate mathematical proofs, there is currently little evidence that they can pose fruitful questions or open up profound new fields of mathematics."" That statement is correct, but Delip Rao turns it around: 'A system that cannot yet ask profound questions has already solved a millennium prize problem.'"" Moreover, he argues that this ability to solve well-defined problems is even more critical for machine learning research than for pure mathematics.""The core of mathematical research is to expand human.

understanding of concepts, proposing new frameworks like topology or group theory , which is more fundamental than solving problems. But in AI research, the priorities are reversed; experimentalists only care if a new recipe can practically train a model to be smarter, not whether the theory is elegant.""The progress of deep learning over the past 15 years hasn't really relied on new theories.""He gives a very specific example: the Transformer."" This architecture, which defines the entire era of large language models, had all its core components known before the 2017 paper was published. Researchers active at the time were well aware that attention mechanisms could improve. parallel training and allow information to pass through longer sequences."" Chris Olah was in that circle back then ; he feels the Transformer simply combined existing, effective ideas in a rather radical and natural way.""So why wasn't it invented sooner?""Because this architecture required five or six additional tweaks before it could significantly outperform the best solutions of that time.""Almost all the parts had been sitting in the literature for years, but no one knew exactly how to put them together. This requires excellent research taste and a massive number of small experiments; consistently and smartly testing dozens. of combinations is precisely the strength AI has shown in mathematics."" His conclusion is straightforward: since AlexNet sparked the deep learning revolution in 2012, the biggest breakthrough in machine learning has been the Transformer. And something like this could be invented by a model at the level of Claude 3, provided Chris Olah asked it to work extremely hard on improving the attention mechanism.""Of course, some aspects of AI research are harder to verify than math. Otherwise, if we clearly have models capable of autonomously solving millennium problems , why haven't we fired all the researchers yet?""His judgment is that the verifiability of AI research is. already high enough.""If he had to choose a median year for automated researchers to reach the level of top human experts, he would choose 2028, assuming labs keep moving at full speed , don't proactively slow down, and aren't suppressed by the government. Why could it be done within a few years?"" The reason he gives is that in every field where answers can be verified and AI can practice for thousands of rounds , AI has gone from being worse than most people to surpassing the very best in just a few short years." It’s the same for programming competitions and solving clear-cut math problems; the model’s generalization ability goes far beyond its direct training. OpenAI's model wasn't built by grinding through other. millennium prize problems; it was trained on vast amounts of easier math and then directly transferred to unsolved ones. He also acknowledges the flip side: some crucial aspects are indeed difficult to automate. It’s hard to predict this in advance, but he estimates there is at least a 25%chance that this won't be achieved until after 2030. But conversely, it could be much faster. Some well-informed researchers he knows, who have had great track records in the past few years, believe AI could surpass top-tier humans in AI research as early as next year. Taking the conclusion that progress has doubled and plugging it directly into "takeoff"

models also points to around 2027. Ajeya Cotra, who has been on his show, once said that if we accept the claim that AI is nearly doubling its own rate of progress, and assume this acceleration happens smoothly. Then the most direct inference is that we will reach extreme superintelligence within a year. He hasn't set 2027 as the median simply because he’s not quite confident in such straightforward models, but in his own words, we shouldn't be surprised if we hit this milestone next year; we should be prepared. Once AI’s research capabilities match the very best humans , why would progress accelerate so. drastically? He gave three reasons: faster, smarter, and more. First, speed : today’s AI works about ten times faster than humans, and automated researchers don't need to sleep, working nights and weekends. Altogether, each automated researcher’s weekly output is about 50 times that of a human. Of course, that doesn't mean AI progress will immediately accelerate 50-fold; experimental compute is still a bottleneck, so experiments won't run faster, leading to diminishing returns. But even with steep diminishing returns , algorithmic progress will still be several times faster. Next, smarter: his sense is that at a frontier lab, about. 80%of algorithmic progress comes from the top 50 researchers. It’s no wonder Mark Zuckerberg is willing to spend hundreds of millions of dollars to recruit the best talent. In an automated company, where every researcher and engineer reaches the level of today’s top humans, that in itself is another significant acceleration. Finally, quantity: the "human sea" tactic isn't a cure-all; for instance, having a group of agents write a novel isn't necessarily much faster than one agent. But some tasks are inherently suited for parallelism. His video features an animation of a group of agents collaborating to turn Fermat's Last Theorem into a formal proof. The project. has thousands of modular subtasks that can be advanced independently, with each agent able to verify its own work on the spot. AI research is more like proving theorems than writing novels; it has plenty of independent modular work and verifiable progress metrics, where 1,000 methods can be tested simultaneously to see which is best, and this can be done at every stage of the process. He doesn't shy away from the fact that there are diminishing returns here— 100,000 collaborators don't mean a 100,000 x speedup; it probably wouldn't even be 100x. However, given the nature of AI research, he also finds it implausible that increasing labor by several orders of magnitude wouldn't even result in a several-fold speedup. Next is the most interesting part of the entire argument: will this speed be maintained, continue to accelerate, or slow down? He says this question is even more important than how fast the initial speed is. There are two opposing forces here: one is Recursive Self-Improvement (RSI), where automated researchers will keep getting faster, smarter, and more numerous. The other force is that good ideas are becoming increasingly hard to find. Note that this is already happening: AI companies have to quadruple their annual R&D compute and double their headcount just to maintain the same rate of progress. If the speed at which AI gets smarter outpaces the.

speed at which ideas get harder to find , we will see what is called a "pure software takeoff." In this scenario, even without adding any more compute, the AI collective will rapidly iterate into increasingly smarter versions of itself. They would become superintelligences that push against the physical limits of current chips within a few short months. Conversely, if ideas get harder to find faster, the result is what he calls a "Sparks" scenario: one calendar year yields progress that would take three to six years at current speeds, and then everything slows down until we build more compute. This is because even these super-genius-level automated researchers need to run. larger-scale experiments to continue making breakthroughs. He estimates the probability of these two scenarios at roughly half and half—50%for "Sparks" and 50%for "pure software takeoff." But to be clear, even in the "Sparks" scenario, things are crazy enough: the first calendar year after AI research automation is roughly equivalent to 4 years of progress, meaning we would cover the span from GPT-3.5 to GPT-6/ SOTA in just 12 months. What level is GPT-3.5 at? It’s a passable coder that can complete a simple Python function, but is otherwise basically a useless toy ; whereas SOTA models can build complete video games from scratch and produce so. many mathematical contributions that we’ve become numb to it. In the past four years, we have gone from a preschooler to a genius student. If we span a similarly large interval starting from 2027 or 2028, we will likely achieve an intelligence that far surpasses humans in any field that is even slightly verifiable. Designing the next generation of AI accelerators, it will outperform NVIDIA; given equal market access, it will be more profitable than any human-run startup or firm today. Give it remote control over a materials science lab to find room-temperature superconductors, and it will be better at it than the rest of. humanity combined. You might ask, how could a superintelligence trained in a data center possibly defeat human experts in fields that require years of real-world experience? After all, our current way of making AI smarter relies on tasks that can be automatically graded in data centers, such as writing code to pass unit tests or solving open-ended math problems. How do you train an AI to start a business, win a lawsuit, execute a profitable daily trade, or help a candidate win an election? The processes for these tasks require interaction with the real world and cannot be replicated in a server room. His answer is not to expect to. bake the answers to every real-world problem directly into the model, but rather to focus on the ability to quickly master new situations, even in these hard-to-verify fields. Accomplishing tasks requires two things : domain knowledge and a set of more general skills—the kind that capable people share, such as finding relevant information, planning, pushing forward through errors and obstacles, documenting what is learned, and collaborating with others. During recursive self-improvement, automation engineers will build reinforcement learning environments that are tens of thousands of times more complex than today’s—larger in scale, longer in duration, higher in quality, and more.

open-ended. AI will have to learn to navigate an unimaginably large number of virtual worlds; compared to today’s video games, these would be like a Bugatti compared to a horse-drawn carriage. They will be harder, messier, larger, and closer to reality than anything built for human entertainment, and they will require AI to cooperate or compete with other AI teams over long periods. For instance, throw an AI into a simulated economy with millions of other AIs and task it with co-founding a successful company. It won't just dwell on idealized company structures; instead , it will undergo the equivalent of centuries of corporate competition to. figure out the best ways to organize. You can use history for backtesting: train it only on data up to 1700 to see if it can derive general relativity, or give it only newspapers up to 1962 to see if it can predict how the Cuban Missile Crisis unfolds. Why should we believe that this training will transfer into general-purpose competence? He provided a very bold analogy about human evolution. Our general cognitive architecture was shaped by evolution, and evolution is a very crude optimization process that simply passes on a set of standard genes. In the ancestral environment, the task of this. standard was hunting, avoiding predators , and maintaining tribal status; these are only a tiny fraction of the tasks humans can handle today. Evolution never specifically optimized us to write code , design advanced semiconductors, lead nations of millions, or pioneer new branches of mathematics; yet, in the process of optimizing for survival on the savanna, it inadvertently created a general-purpose learner. If evolution could accomplish that, AI companies, with clear goals and deliberate training , can certainly go even further. Of course, even smarter learners cannot figure everything out just by staying in. a data center. To surpass the top human experts, they still need a bit of real-world experience. However, he predicts that the speed at which AI gains experience will far exceed people's expectations, surpassing top human experts within months of deployment. There are plenty of examples of this. Napoleon was 27 when he had already defeated much larger armies of European powers, and Rockefeller had only been in the oil industry for two years before running one of the world's largest refineries. They did need experience, but it took years, not decades. Whatever happened in their minds, AI should be able to replicate or even surpass it; there is no reason to. believe humans have reached the ceiling for how fast one can learn from experience. Moreover, AI has another advantage: it can accumulate years of deployment experience in just a few calendar days. If you want a future AI to manage a Fortune 500 company better than the current CEO, how long would it take to get up to speed? On the first morning, have it shadow the CEO, and it could read every email, every instant message, and every document in the company's history. By the end of the first day, its multiple avatars could have interviewed every employee and major client. It indeed cannot access feedback that requires months of waiting.

, such as next quarter's financial results, but even with this limitation, he still expects such AI to reach top-tier human levels in all fields within months of its development. According to his median scenario, that is something that will happen in 2028 or 2029. And the story doesn't end there; even if progress at the software level gradually plateaus, AI will continue to improve by increasing computing power. Over the past five years, even without any AI assistance, global AI computing power has roughly tripled every year. AI created by sparks will be particularly adept at helping us continue to scale up. compute—for example, by designing new AI chips, planning new power plants, or even remotely controlling robots to build facilities and data centers. The only difference is that this path takes years to reach the same destination that purely hardware-based approaches could reach in just a few months. This superintelligence, which relates to humans as we relate to chimpanzees—for this video, I’ve included a technical argument at the end to explain why AI research is, in principle, verifiable. This part is a bit hard-core, so I’ll summarize the key points for you. AI R& D is roughly divided into three main areas: pre-training, post-training, and inference efficiency, each with concrete metrics that can serve directly as. training objectives. These three areas combined perfectly cover the entirety of algorithmic progress. So, it’s not surprising that overall AI progress can be used as a training objective; since AI training happens inside data centers , the things we do to improve models are exactly what data centers can measure. First, let’s look at pre-training: you can set a target for a model to reach a fixed loss on a small-scale model using as little compute as possible. Loss on a test set is a measurable value, very easy to verify, and even rankable. You can design an environment to see if the model can predict whether algorithmic. improvements that work at one parameter scale will still hold true at a scale of 10 billion parameters. Post-training also has proxy metrics, such as dropping a model into an environment it has never seen to see how quickly it adapts to achieve good results; ByteDance’s AdaBench benchmark measures exactly this type of capability. Inside ByteDance, there is also a benchmark called "C," which contains about 500 real-world problems that their researchers and engineers have solved this year. Every benchmark is also a reinforcement learning environment, which essentially tasks the model with replicating the frontier progress humans have made in the last three to six months; inference. efficiency is even easier to measure, as GPU usage, KV cache size per token, and latency are all readily available numbers. Tucked inside this is a counterintuitive piece of information: the lab Magic recently announced that they used about half the compute of the original GPT-3 to train a foundational model capable of rivaling leading open-weights models like DeepSeek-V 4 Pro. At today’s prices, that amount of compute is worth approximately $ 500,000 . So he concludes that pre-training hasn't hit a ceiling; increasing it by several orders of magnitude is entirely possible. Finally, let's see how he addresses the harshest criticism, namely the three strongest arguments against.

recursive self-improvement. First point : continual learning. For the past year and a half, he has maintained that the core capability AI lacks today is learning from work experience. Every new session is like its first day on the job ; a session can only retain a few hours of information, failing to accumulate the feedback and know-how that takes weeks or months to build. In December 2025, he was still saying it was incredible that these systems, lacking even the basic learning abilities of a child, were trying to crack the AGI algorithms that have baffled humanity for over half a century. But now he's changed his tune, for two reasons. First , solving continual learning might not. require a major architectural breakthrough; scaling up in-context learning to make sessions effectively last longer, allowing a single instance to learn while it works, might be enough . Second, continual learning is itself a research problem with clear validation metrics, similar to solving a math problem. If you had asked him two years ago to compare the Navier-Stokes equations with continual learning, asking which is harder to solve, he wouldn't have thought the answer was obviously the former. His analogy is clever: current models lack long-term memory, like the clumsiest interns, yet they are already solving millennial-old problems. It's like someone moving down the track while doing cartwheels, yet. still keeping pace with Usain Bolt. Who says that doing cartwheels means they can't win the race? However, he still leaves room for doubt; if we fail to solve continual learning in the next few years, and models can't compensate with other advantages, that remains a serious possibility. That is why he gave a 25% probability that automating top-tier research at the level of Ilya Sutskever won't happen until after 2032. Second point: data. Data is the primary input for AI progress. If data doesn't keep up , how can recursive self-improvement occur? His answer is that the entity compiling the data is the AI itself. He conducted research with Princeton. student Jerry Han, finding that over the past six years of pre-training progress , gains from data improvements outweighed gains from model improvements by more than three times. And so-called data improvement is essentially figuring out which methods can filter existing data and generate new synthetic data to lower the loss function, which is very similar to regular AI research work. A paper published on post-training new models confirms this; they found that systematic improvements in the scale, diversity, and verifiability of synthetic data environments basically account for all observed gains. And the way these environments are constructed. is itself becoming increasingly automated. Third, experimental compute. While mathematics can produce new discoveries with just a pen and paper, AI research requires running actual experiments, burning both compute and time. As the number of researchers grows , won't the experimental compute allocated to each person become diluted ? He did the math: if labs increase their compute by more than four times each year, following this trend, by the end of 2027, OpenAI could provide 10,000 agents—the same number of agents involved in solving that millennial prize problem. Every agent would be able to be allocated enough compute to run a GPT-3 scale training session every single day. The final model in the.

original 2017 Transformer paper only used 8 P100s for three days; that amount of compute costs about 50 dollars today , which is only one ten-thousandth of the compute used to train GPT-3. If researchers like Ilya and X2 had the experimental compute to train a GPT-3 scale model every day, they might be a bit slower than they are now. But if they just sat there and couldn't produce any meaningful progress, only complaining that the cluster was too small, he would be very surprised. Moreover, the reason labs use compute the way they do today is because researchers 'time is far scarcer than compute; the annual compensation for top researchers can reach hundreds of. millions of dollars. The way we use it today doesn't show how efficient it could be once compute becomes the main bottleneck. Agent swarms have two advantages humans can't match: first, trading labor for compute—reading every training trajectory, and as soon as a task breaks, immediately stopping to rebuild the entire environment. Small-scale experiments can be run relentlessly. Before pooling compute for a large experiment, we should spend subjective decades designing the most information-dense joint experiments, then spend another subjective few decades analyzing the results to invent better scientific methods, extracting every bit of information from small experiments. The GPT-4 paper stated that they could predict the loss of the final. model using a model with 10,000 times less compute. Scaling phenomena like this allow researchers to predict optimal hyperparameters for large training runs from models 100 times smaller. He remembers a conversation with a researcher who once said: the gods above must surely follow the same principles as the ants below. After hearing the whole argument, you’ll find his position is actually more restrained than the title suggests. The median year is set to 2028, with room left for 2027 and after 2032, splitting the probability of software-only and "spark " at 50%each. What he really wants to say is that recursive self-improvement. might have already started. So, do you think his judgment is correct? Feel free to leave a comment below. 值得閱讀的理由

  • 破除誇大迷思：由 OpenAI 首位首席經濟學家的權威視角，理性剖析 AI 帶來「10% 經濟暴衝」與「失業率短期暴增三倍」等不切實際的預測。

摘要

破除 AI 經濟神話：理性看待成長與失業衝擊

作者大飛指出，圍繞當前 AI 熱潮的兩大極端預測——10% 的經濟成長率以及短期內失業率暴增三倍——在 OpenAI 首位首席經濟學家 Ronnie Chatterji 眼中均不切實際。Chatterji 認為，美國經濟只要增加 1% 至 2% 的成長率就已是翻天覆地的變革，而失業率哪怕僅微幅上升 0.5 到 1 個百分點，便足以引發嚴重的社會動盪；將 2020 年因疫情全面封城的極端經驗套用於未來 12 到 18 個月的 AI 衝擊，本質上是基準校準的錯誤。

從晶片法案到 OpenAI：首席經濟學家的職責與布局

曾深度參與美國《晶片法案》（CHIPS Act）推動的 Chatterji，在與 OpenAI 探討半導體議題的過程中，親手撰寫了首席經濟學家的職務描述，最終因緣際會親自接下該重任。他打造了一支融合經濟學博士、數據科學家與具備跨部門推進力的MBA 專案經理團隊。頂尖 AI 實驗室引進經濟學家的目的，除了將龐大的用戶數據解讀給商務部或各國央行等決策機構外，更關鍵的是研究未來工作者管理AI Agent（代理人）時，所催生出的全新組織行為與激勵機制。

未來 12 至 18 個月的趨勢：深層系統串接與職能界線模糊

展望未來一年半的局勢，Chatterji 提出三大核心觀察：第一，AI 革命才剛要深度滲透企業，關鍵在於跨出問答機器人形式，將連接器（Connectors）深度整合至現有企業系統中；第二，就業市場不會直接面臨全面淘汰，而是工作實質內容的轉變，許多員工已開始跨出既有職務描述，例如財務人員執行行銷任務、公關人員自主跑數據；第三，龐大的硬體資本支出已率先推動 GDP 數字，但實質的生產力躍升將在未來一年多內陸續浮現於統計數據中。

法務與人資的逆勢突圍與全球 AI 版圖的分歧

undermine the authority of human experts , which is a valid concern, but many overlook the scenario where AI acts as the first expert. exposure. Interestingly, he feels the hottest-growing industries aren't growing as fast as he thought, while some unassuming sectors are changing quietly. 破除 AI 經濟神話：理性看待成長與失業衝擊

從晶片法案到 OpenAI：首席經濟學家的職責與布局

曾深度參與美國《晶片法案》（CHIPS Act）推動的 Chatterji，在與 OpenAI 探討半導體議題的過程中，親手撰寫了首席經濟學家的職務描述，最終因緣際會親自接下該重任。他打造了一支融合經濟學博士、數據科學家與具備跨部門推進力的MBA 專案經理團隊。頂尖 AI 實驗室引進經濟學家的目的，除了將龐大的用戶數據解讀給商務部或各國央行等決策機構外，更關鍵的是研究未來工作者管理AI Agent（代理人）時，所催生出的全新組織行為與激勵機制。

未來 12 至 18 個月的趨勢：深層系統串接與職能界線模糊

展望未來一年半的局勢，Chatterji 提出三大核心觀察：第一，AI 革命才剛要深度滲透企業，關鍵在於跨出問答機器人形式，將連接器（Connectors）深度整合至現有企業系統中；第二，就業市場不會直接面臨全面淘汰，而是工作實質內容的轉變，許多員工已開始跨出既有職務描述，例如財務人員執行行銷任務、公關人員自主跑數據；第三，龐大的硬體資本支出已率先推動 GDP 數字，但實質的生產力躍升將在未來一年多內陸續浮現於統計數據中。

法務與人資的逆勢突圍與全球 AI 版圖的分歧

在企業內部落地節奏上，Chatterji 觀察到法務與人資部門因具備密集的流程與豐富的結構化數據，轉型速度出乎意料地名列前茅；以 OpenAI 內部為例，非技術部門全面深度整合 AI 僅比技術團隊落後約四至五個月。放大至全球格局，日本與南韓依託強大的晶片供應鏈與人口結構挑戰積極擁抱 AI；印尼與巴西則受惠於 18 至 25 歲的年輕人口紅利，展現超乎預期的活躍度；歐洲則深陷於科技自主架構與監管平衡的激烈辯論。為真實評測勞動力替代情況，OpenAI 亦推出依據美國勞工部 O*NET 架構的 JDBench 基準測試，藉由 44 種真實職業情境精準檢驗模型的實務能力。

Hello everyone, this is Best Partners, I’m Da Fei. If I had to pick the two most modest numbers for this AI boom, they would probably be these: 10% economic growth and a tripling of the unemployment rate in the short term. One feels like a windfall from the sky, the other like the ground cracking beneath your feet. For the past two years, almost every discussion about AI has circled back to these two figures. OpenAI's first chief economist, Ronnie Chatterji, offers a calm judgment: neither of these two numbers is likely to happen. In his view, even an extra percentage point of growth in the US economy would be transformative; two. more points, and everyone would feel it in their daily lives. Why is he skeptical about using the same model to project. AI's impact over the next 12 to 18 months? That’s what we’re going to talk about today. Chatterji is OpenAI’s first chief economist, having been in the role for about two years. This position didn't actually exist at first; he had just finished his term in government, where he participated in the rollout of the CHIPS Act. He initially talked with OpenAI about chips and semiconductors. After several rounds of discussions and working with different groups of people , the topic shifted to a specific need: the company needed a chief economist. His response at the time was blunt: "I don't want the job, but I can help you write a job description." Later, when OpenAI came back to him with that job. description, seeing that they handed him the very document he had written, he realized he had the chance to shape the role exactly as he wanted. After consulting with his wife, he felt this was an opportunity he couldn't pass up. The job description was revised about six times, but two things never changed from the start. First, the research must be beneficial to people and provide the public with accurate information about AI. Because this position receives so much attention, anything released will surely be under intense scrutiny. Therefore, there is a responsibility to ensure that the outside world receives the right judgments. Second, there must be a team capable of delivering results. . He wants people with PhDs and data science backgrounds, but also people who are capable of driving things forward within the organization. Having worked in government, I know how hard it is to push things across departments, so I specifically recruited people with MBA backgrounds who have actually managed projects. In the end, this team was formed by a mix of project managers, data scientists, and economists. Tech companies hiring economists began roughly at the start of this century. When Hal Varian was still teaching at Berkeley, Chatterjee was his student and used his textbooks. Later, when Varian joined Google, the academic world was. shaken; back then, academics joining corporations was extremely rare. Later on, more and more economists entered tech firms. So why does a frontier lab need someone like this? The first reason is data. Beyond a handful of global institutions, we possess some of the richest data on AI usage in the consumer sector. This data needs to be interpreted and presented to institutions like the Department of Commerce or the Bank of England to help them understand what is happening in the industry. Although the company has a top-tier data science team, data scientists usually focus on product decisions; we need someone to step out.

of the lab and look at the broader socioeconomic structure. The second reason is even more novel: the company is creating a new class of economic participants. His hypothesis is that the next generation of workers will likely manage more AI agents than human colleagues. What exactly are the behavioral patterns of these agents? What kind of organizational structures will they spawn, and what incentive mechanisms should be used to regulate them? Economists have a ready-made toolkit for these questions. Looking at the next 12 to 18 months, he predicts three things will happen, and they are already emerging. First, the revolution will truly penetrate enterprises. He. says we are still at a very early stage . This might sound strange to say in San Francisco, but in the rest of the world , it is indeed just getting started. If we look at companies using AI now, the proportion that have truly enabled connectors to integrate AI into existing software is still very small. Yet this step is crucial; if AI doesn't have access to your computers and systems and is just a Q&A bot, its value clearly cannot be realized. Second, the job market won't change as drastically as many expect; what will change is the work content beneath the surface. He offered an observation: a large portion of work has already moved beyond job descriptions—for instance, finance. people are now handling marketing tasks , and corporate communications staff can run their own data. People are stepping outside their job boundaries to do things they’ve never done before. As more people in companies gain access to agents, this trend will only accelerate . Regarding productivity statistics, he said that AI has already entered GDP through capital expenditure, with hardware investment on a massive scale. However, economists are really eyeing productivity, and he expects more significant changes in this area over the next 12 to 18 months. As for the discussion about those two inflated numbers, they are essentially the same issue regarding our calibration of scale. . Moving on, the host asked a question that is easily overlooked: which department will actually make the first move? Chatterjee’s answer was somewhat counterintuitive. He said that legal and human resources—two departments many feel are far removed from AI—should not be underestimated. Within OpenAI, he observed the legal department transforming its workflow with AI as quickly as any team he has ever seen. He added a caveat that the legal profession itself is a biased sample and cannot fully represent the outside world. Regarding the pace of internal corporate adoption, using OpenAI as an example: in November 2025, various groups in San Francisco were having heated discussions. , with people sharing amazing use cases , but it wasn't until April and May 2026 that non-research and non-engineering departments became as deeply integrated with AI as the technical teams. He himself didn't fully start utilizing it until that time. According to him, as an economist with so many degrees who does data analysis every day, he is still classified as "non-technical" in the company system. Therefore, there is roughly a four to five-month lag between technical and non-technical departments . He emphasized that not every company is like OpenAI, but functions like legal and HR, which are process-intensive with abundant structured data, are what he. will be focusing on. The gap between enterprises is also widening. Some companies have already tapped into the potential of their internal super-users , while the so-called median adopters are still a long way from that step. This gap is not only widening, but it will also directly impact how much AI can be converted into economic results. When scaled to the national level, the divergence is even greater. Japan and South Korea are optimistic about AI's ability to transform the economy, driven by their past technological successes, demographics different from the West, and a group of companies that have already tasted the benefits. Looking at South Korea’s chip supply chain, with SK Hynix and Samsung leading the way, the effects are clearly visible. Enterprises.

in these regions are heavy users of AI, and because they were already connected to other technologies, the adoption of generative AI has been very smooth. A positive surprise is Indonesia and Brazil, where usage rates are much higher than he expected. Ou will release the relevant data, attributing a large part of the reason to a young population . People aged 18 to 25 are high-frequency AI users, a pattern seen globally. In Jakarta universities, he saw students discussing AI at a level almost identical to San Francisco, with no sense of lag. India is no longer a surprise; he attended an AI conference and was still deeply struck by the number of companies emerging around AI. More interesting are the large corporate groups. Having studied business school cases, they don't want to be the dinosaurs that get disrupted and are working hard to ensure they use AI. At the other end is Europe, where the struggle is two-fold: how to generate productivity from AI in enterprises, and how to safeguard core segments of their key tech stack amid globalization's retreat and shifting geopolitics. Since the Draghi memorandum was released, the internal debate in Europe has been intense. Chatterjee is reluctant to call it negative; he prefers to describe it as a genuine debate about what role AI should play in business and society. At. this point, the conversation shifted to a topic directly related to whether AI will take away jobs. OpenAI has created a benchmark test called JDBench. It doesn't use test questions, but instead uses real-world work to challenge the models. This is a test where experienced practitioners from 44 professions create questions and grade the models on whether they can do the job. The logic starts with a task list; the U.S. Department of Labor has a system called O*NET that breaks every profession down into individual tasks. With this list, one can ask: "Can AI do this task better than a human?" That is where the problem lies. Many people initially assume that. if a job has ten tasks and AI can do five of them better, then that person has a 50%chance of losing their job. But Chatterjee says that is not how things work at all. Chatterjee gave an example involving his own father. In 1984, his father installed a computer in his office. His father was an economics professor who needed to run large regressions. Before the computer, he had to carry stacks of punch cards into the machine room. Once broken down by task, the computer could do almost every part of the professor's job, but he didn't lose his job in 1984. He used the computer to run bigger regressions, build more models, and write more papers. . This example illustrates one thing: work being covered by AI does not mean being replaced by AI. Sometimes, it is quite the opposite; being covered means you have the opportunity to leverage it . Another reason less often mentioned is that tasks are endogenous; no one tells you to just do these ten things, as you have a higher goal, and tasks emerge to serve that objective. Later, after talking to those who had actually walked that path, he discovered that failure is often where one learns the most, and it can also be the prelude to the next great company. There are also some people who, only after starting a business, realize they are better suited as co-founders or simply working for someone else. Therefore, the faster the process, the better; one of the biggest benefits of AI is that it helps people reach that conclusion more quickly. This means there will be more failures, but fortunately, there will also be more successes, and the path for.

solo-entrepreneurship has been opened up . The part related to AI depends on the hardware supply chain; for example, the price of DRAM memory has risen very sharply over. the past year. He believes that inflation caused by supply chain bottlenecks only accounts for a small piece, and as infrastructure expands and supply catches up, this part will gradually recede, which of course also depends on competition among companies in the chain. In the long run, it suppresses the force AI has to lower prices; it might not be visible within two years, but if we take a longer view , this deflationary effect will be significant. Some call this the "Jevons Paradox," but he prefers to call it a downward-sloping demand curve: if you lower the cost of completing a task, as long as there is enough elasticity, demand will rise, and many markets will expand as a result; he has already seen.

signs of this in his own research. If AI continues to deliver, what would it look like if we jumped straight to 2031? History will repeat itself, perhaps on an even larger scale. Stanford's Nick Bloom, John Van Reenen, and Raffaella Sadun famously analyzed IT adoption in US and UK firms. US firms had higher adoption rates and better management practices, leading to higher productivity—a dividend that boosted the US economy for. years. If the returns on AI are as expected, we will see a similar trajectory: US firms will fully embrace AI and use that capability globally to lift economic growth. An increase of one to two percentage points, or even three to four, would be a massive change. Looking at the employment structure, he predicts massive growth in education and healthcare. The logic is simple: the wealthier a society, the more it spends on education and healthcare. Once the AI dividend arrives, truly important priorities will emerge, with caring for people and educating the next generation at the forefront. Furthermore, history shows that when technology enters these. two fields, it often simultaneously creates a demand for more human labor. However, there is also a preference issue. He says if he had to choose between replacing a kindergarten teacher with a robot or shrinking class sizes so two teachers could instruct half the number of students, he would choose the latter. He believes most Americans feel the same regarding doctors, nurses, and caregivers. The real suspense lies in wages. Education and healthcare account for about one-seventh of US jobs. If we shift the economic focus to these areas but the new positions pay less than previous jobs, there is no gain—so. compensation for these roles must rise. The entertainment industry is another possible engine; he jokes about how many children now say they want to be influencers when they grow up. Economists love to track new job titles . It used to be cybersecurity experts; now it might be influencers. Even the term "podcaster" hasn't been around for very many years. Using AI and other tools to create entertainment and distribute it on platforms like YouTube could also give rise to new media formats we haven't even imagined yet. So the question arises: who pays for the extra teachers, doctors, and nurses? His answer is that if AI truly generates such significant returns, the money will. be there. Part of the solution may involve how we tax labor versus capital . By aligning mechanisms, providing the right incentives, and having rational government channels, we can direct the productivity dividends created by AI into these sectors. But if it is not handled well, we will have to rely on robust institutional safety nets, which is fundamentally a matter of public administration. He made a very pragmatic point: if AI doesn't succeed, we won't even have the foundation to do these things, but in a world where AI is a huge success, there will be abundant funding for education and healthcare. He pointed out a scenario often overlooked : if everyone lets their own agent. compete for scarce resources, will the system get overwhelmed? Chatterjee gave an analogy: suppose everyone uses an agent to book the same popular restaurant, but the restaurant only has one phone line—it would ring incessantly . The solution is for the restaurant to also have an agent platform; both sides need platforms that can communicate with each other. In a future where everyone is competing for scarce resources, if there is an AI platform running on set rules to coordinate, the welfare benefits would be immense. He feels this is one of the most exciting, yet most overlooked, potentials of AI. He also specifically raised another perspective : people are always worried that AI will.

undermine the authority of human experts , which is a valid concern, but many overlook the scenario where AI acts as the first expert. If you cannot find a behavioral health specialist within 100 miles, you are already in a service desert; in this case, having an AI that can listen to you and offer initial advice is incredibly valuable. So, in many places where people have no resources to begin with, AI is actually filling that void. Finally, discussing exports and trade, Chatterjee said the lead department for economic policy has shifted; when he first joined the administration, this work was mostly in the Treasury and the White House, but over the last decade, the Commerce. Department has become a core player, or even the primary one. Chatterjee used an Economics 101 and 102 framework to answer this question. 101 argues that production should happen where costs are lowest and economies of scale are strongest. That is how global semiconductor manufacturing ended up highly concentrated in Taiwan, where TSMC is based. 102 argues that excessive concentration of production in one geographic region creates externalities ; if that region is also in a. geopolitically sensitive area, the externalities aren't just environmental or sustainability issues—they directly involve national security. Therefore, decision-making must be approached with the perspective of 102. Chatterjee’s own judgment is that access to models and intelligence will be important globally , but for frontier capabilities, especially in fields like cybersecurity , countries will be very cautious due to national interests, as power dynamics and security hinge on these things. Economic benefits and national security are, in reality, inseparable. This was also the biggest lesson he learned during his second stint in government. The first time he managed the economy, he barely dealt with national security. or defense officials. The second time he returned, almost everything had become geoeconomics, sitting at the intersection of national security and traditional economic policy. His generation of economists was not trained this way. He recalls asking a professor about industrial policy on his first day , only to be told that it was something for Europeans to worry about and the U.S. didn't need to bother. When he returned to government, he was racking his brain on how to rebuild a vibrant semiconductor manufacturing industry on U.S. soil. He believes this shift will span multiple sectors; AI, quantum computing, energy, and biology will all face the same issues. There is another change many people haven't realized: the. market logic of deep tech is different from the internet era. In the past, people were accustomed to using the global population to estimate the total addressable market. But once the market splits into several independent strategic camps, the math changes. The mission of the internet era was to bring more people in; the core problem for quantum computing is who breaks through first and whose technology is the strongest. When the underlying logic changes, the total market size changes too. So, how can an economist at a single company make people believe their research is neutral? After taking office, he immediately realized that he had to bring in outside scholars . There are two reasons: first, academia can see things outside his field of vision. By opening a window for scholars under compliance and security frameworks , their insights can, in turn, inspire him. It’s impossible to have top experts in every niche field on the team, so leveraging external help is a must. They must publish publicly. The way economists communicate is through working papers and journals. Although those things sound old-fashioned, if you want to truly influence academia's understanding of AI, you have to write them. Even though the publication and.

review cycle for papers is long, once published, it lays a new layer of knowledge onto the entire discipline. He mentioned a working paper of his that was cited 850 times in less than a year , meaning 850 scholars believe this research is worth building upon. To put the outside world at ease, the team also did a few things. First, they made underlying data as public as possible so anyone wanting to run regressions or verify findings could do so. By going through rigorous peer review, having papers accepted by top journals at least shows that the broader academic community outside of the company also recognizes this rigor. Furthermore, they support others in conducting research rather than doing everything themselves. . They have a program called "Exchange, " which has funded 14 teams so far to conduct research using OpenAI's data with complete academic independence. The "Superalignment" team follows the same logic, with OpenAI bringing in Jason Furman and Michael Strain—one leaning left and the other right. His point is that even when economists have vastly different political stances, they still share a consensus on 85%of the fundamentals, with disagreements mainly centered on the frontier. In the future , billions of people will turn to AI every day for financial advice, news, and interpersonal relations; such a system must be neutral and evidence-based. Judgment criteria vary greatly among different people and. groups; only by inviting authorities from various schools of thought can trust be built. He specifically named Daron Acemoglu as the person he most wants to review OpenAI's data. This professor holds quite a few critical views on AI. While some might see that as dangerous, Zhatji’s attitude is quite the opposite, seeing it as motivation to identify and fill gaps. He is eager to share the underlying data with him without reservation and is curious to see if they will arrive at the same conclusions after the analysis. He expects there will still be differences in interpreting long-term trends, but when it comes to rigorous argumentation using solid data, Acemoglu is the ideal partner for debate. He said that while he used to be the teacher on the podium, through these visits, he has instead become the student. That is why he values face-to-face interaction so much; if you only argue on social media, it's easy to forget a basic truth, whereas when you are truly standing in front of someone, it is hard to be malicious. So, why doesn't this team conduct long-term forecasting? He said that trade-offs were necessary when building the team. They wanted to do everything at first, but experienced colleagues at OpenAI. advised him to cut some things back. The final principle decided upon was to focus on the present and focus on solid data. This also relates to his experience in government. Having sat in the seat of a policymaker, he knows that what officials and executives lack most isn't an imagination for 2035, but an understanding of what is happening right now. Long-term predictions can be overturned every six months, with implementation timelines constantly pushed back. Conversely, an empirical study that clearly explains how AI is impacting the job market right now is much more useful. Of course, there is a cost; upon release, the outside world might feel the conclusions offer nothing new, but before that, such intuition had. no data to back it up. In such a fast-changing era, making accurate predictions is difficult. When asked what the economy will be able to do in 2036 that it can't today, his answer was the emergence of truly intelligent organizations. Additionally, he checks one figure every week: revenue per employee. It's not for the entire industry, but for a group of companies he selected that have high AI.

exposure. Interestingly, he feels the hottest-growing industries aren't growing as fast as he thought, while some unassuming sectors are changing quietly. Although we don't see drastic changes in the short term, we know change is hidden within job boundaries, in the substance of organizational changes over four to five months, and in a productivity curve that hasn't turned yet. He says the road to AGI must pass through our organizations. Everyone is fixated on model capabilities, thinking that if it. can do something, it will be done, but they forget that for technology to be implemented, it must go through the organizational layer. So what we should really pay attention to might not be which benchmark scores a model just refreshed, but when your company integrates AI into real business processes and whether your own job boundaries have begun to expand.   • 說明中國經濟增長與股市、企業獲利表現背離的原因，帶讀者看見數字背後的結構問題。

  • 介紹 AI、出海與反內卷等潛在成長動能，以及不同產業的獲利前景與投資風險。

摘要

經濟增長，為何沒有轉化成股市獲利？

作者介紹高盛的中國股票策略報告，並指出疫情以來中國美元計價 GDP 增加約五兆美元，但中國股票表現仍大幅落後全球股市。上市公司的營收與獲利增長放緩，獲利減速尤其明顯；MSCI 中國指數的每股盈餘多年不及預期，股東權益報酬率也持續下滑。股價下跌與本益比收縮，反映出市場對企業盈利能力的疑慮。

作者指出，問題不僅是需求不足或產能過剩，更深層的原因是資本成本被系統性壓低。資金過於便宜，使回報不佳的企業和項目仍能持續取得融資，資源無法有效退出或轉向更具效率的用途。

壓低資本成本的五項因素

報告歸納出五項彼此交織的因素：政府補貼、低息貸款與隱性擔保讓低回報項目得以延續；對正常利潤的政策約束，可能促使企業放棄利潤追求、轉而競逐銷量與市占；資源偏向供給端與製造業，則加劇供需失衡。與此同時，房地產下行削弱總需求，而 AI、自動化等技術進步雖提升效率，也可能帶來價格下跌，使企業面臨「技術更強、價格更難上漲」的局面。

未來獲利的可能動能

作者轉述高盛對未來獲利的推估：未來十年每股盈餘的基準年增率約為 8%，若AI、出海與反內卷形成合力，未來五年年複合增長率有望達到約 10%。報告估計中國企業的穩態 ROE 約為 12%；若市場激勵機制維持，且分紅與回購延續，股市估值可能有約 10% 至 15% 的修復空間。

高盛將中國上市公司與 47 個行業分成結構性成長、穩定成長、估值下修成長、週期成長及低迷成長五類。作者指出，企業盈利增長整體減速，但成長差距正在擴大，市場更重視成長的確定性；結構性成長的代表也逐漸從傳統互聯網與消費產業，轉向AI 硬體、半導體及出口相關產業。

排除房地產等低迷產業後，其餘類別的獲利增長表現更具韌性。高盛預估 2026 至 2028 年結構性成長板塊的每股盈餘年複合增長率約為 30%，高於穩定成長板塊的約 7%。作者提到，AI 硬體與海外市場是結構性成長的重要方向，而相關板塊估值已明顯壓縮，市場悲觀預期可能已有部分反映。

作者總結，中國市場的成長機會正變得更集中，投資環境將由全面普漲轉為產業與公司的結構性分化。AI、企業出海與反內卷能否改善企業利潤，將左右未來幾年的每股盈餘增長；在尋找高成長機會的同時，避開長期低迷的產業也同樣重要。
